newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: FOCUS-Malaysia budget seen boosting finance stocks.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Malaysia budget seen boosting finance stocks.

text.p: The financial sector is set to lead the Malaysian stock market revival following new measures to promote the sector introduced in the 1997 national budget, analysts said on Monday.
The local bourse, after languishing for most of the year, is likely to move in a positive direction as the economy slows down and domestic interest rates head lower, they said.
Deputy Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said on Monday more measures for the financial services sector were introduced because growth in the sector had lagged other sectors.
Anwar, who is also Finance Minister, said growth in the sector has remained the same for the past 10 to 12 years.

Among the new measures announced by Anwar during the budget presentation were permision for stockbroking firms to set up unit trusts, undertake fund management and underwriting, issue call warrants and manage listing of companies, to introduce a zero-coupon bond to provide a benchmark yield curve to stimulate the moribund debt market and allowing private firms to issue ringgit bonds.

He also said foreign fund managers can take up to a 49 percent equity stake in local brokerages and that an over-the-counter (OTC) market will be established to trade shares in new high technology companies.

"Stockbrokers are set to attract investors attention not only due to the potentially wider earnings base but also for its new fund-mobilising activities which are poised to provide additionalliquidity to the whole stock market," Mayban Securities Research said in a report on the budget.

Analysts said the high-technology sector should also benefit from the budget with the establishment of an OTC and incentives announced for companies investing in a multimedia zone that Malaysia is establishing to attract world class information technology firms.
Companies seen benefitting from this include Lityan Holdings Bhd, MCSB Systems (Malaysia) Bhd, Dataprep Holdings Bhd and Fujitsu Systems Business (Malaysia) Bhd.

Losers are likely to include heavy equipment and shipping companies following a proposed five to 20 percent import duty on heavy machinery and withdrawal of double taxation cuts on shipping costs which was implemented last year.
"The abolition of this incentive will mean that Malaysian shipping companies will have to compete on a more level ground with foreign vessels," HLG Securities said in a report.

Analysts said the expected narrowing of the current account deficit and a soft landing for economic growth should erase market disappointment that an expected corporate tax cut did not materialise. Market players had anticipated a one-to-two percent cut in corporate tax from the current 30 percent.
Seow Choong Liang, head of research at Kleinworth Benson Research (Malaysia), said foreign funds should return to the Malaysian market as doubts about the economy eased.
"The overheating problem is more or less over," he said.
Seow believes that local interest rates have peaked and should gradually begin to ease towards end of the year. ($1 = 2.50 ringgit)
